content: Nystatin is an antifungal medication approved by the FDA for the treatment of various fungal infections, including candidal vulvovaginitis, skin candidiasis, cutaneous and mucocutaneous infections, gastrointestinal candidiasis (non-esophageal), and oropharyngeal candidiasis. Common side effects include skin irritation and hypersensitivity reactions. Adult Indications and Dosage: 1. FDA-Labeled Indications: Nystatin cream is used for treating cutaneous or mucocutaneous fungal infections caused by Candida albicans and other susceptible Candida species. It is not intended for systemic, oral, intravaginal, or ophthalmic use. Dosage: Intravaginal tablet: 1 tablet (100,000 units) daily for 2 weeks. Topical cream or ointment: Apply liberally to affected areas twice daily until healing is complete. Topical powder: Apply to candidal lesions 2-3 times daily until healing is complete. For fungal infections of the feet, footwear should also be dusted. Oral tablet: 1-2 tablets (500,000 to 1,000,000 units) orally three times daily. Continue treatment for at least 48 hours after clinical cure. Oral suspension: 4-6 mL (400,000 to 600,000 units) orally, retained in the mouth as long as possible before swallowing, four times daily. Continue treatment for at least 48 hours after symptoms resolve. For HIV patients, treat for 7-14 days. 2. Off-Label Use: Limited information is available regarding off-label use in adults, whether guideline-supported or not. Pediatric Indications and Dosage: 1. FDA-Labeled Indications: Topical cream or ointment: Apply liberally to affected areas twice daily until healing is complete. Topical powder: Apply to candidal lesions 2-3 times daily until healing is complete. For fungal infections of the feet, footwear should also be dusted. Oral suspension for infants: 2 mL (200,000 units) orally four times daily. Continue treatment for at least 48 hours after symptoms resolve. Oral suspension for children: 4-6 mL (400,000 to 600,000 units) orally, retained in the mouth as long as possible before swallowing, four times daily. Continue treatment for at least 48 hours after symptoms resolve. For HIV patients, treat for 7-14 days. 2. Off-Label Use: Limited information is available regarding off-label use in pediatric patients, whether guideline-supported or not. Contraindications: Nystatin cream is contraindicated in patients with a history of hypersensitivity to any of its components. Warnings and Precautions: 1. General: Nystatin cream should not be used for systemic, oral, intravaginal, or ophthalmic infections. If irritation or sensitization occurs, discontinue treatment and take appropriate measures. Diagnostic methods such as KOH smears or cultures should confirm the diagnosis of candidiasis and rule out other pathogens. 2. Patient Information: Patients should use the medication as directed, including replacing missed doses. This medication is only for the condition prescribed and should not be used for other disorders. Even if symptoms improve within the first few days, patients should complete the full course of treatment. If irritation develops, patients should notify their physician promptly. 3. Laboratory Tests: If there is no therapeutic response, diagnostic tests such as KOH smears or cultures should be repeated. Adverse Reactions: Common adverse events include allergic reactions, burning, itching, rash, eczema, and pain at the application site. Pregnancy and Lactation: 1. Pregnancy: Nystatin is classified as Pregnancy Category C. Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted, and it is unknown whether it can cause fetal harm or affect reproductive capacity. It should only be prescribed to pregnant women if the potential benefit outweighs the potential risk to the fetus. There is no Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) guidance on its use during pregnancy. 2. Nursing Mothers: It is unknown whether nystatin is excreted in human milk. Caution should be exercised when prescribing nystatin to nursing women. Use in Specific Populations: 1. Pediatric Use: Safety and effectiveness have been established in pediatric patients from birth to 16 years. 2. Geriatric Use: Clinical studies did not include sufficient numbers of patients aged 65 and older to determine if they respond differently than younger patients. However, greater sensitivity in some older individuals cannot be ruled out. 3. Gender, Race, Renal, and Hepatic Impairment: There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of nystatin in these populations. 4. Immunocompromised Patients: No specific FDA guidance is available for immunocompromised patients. Administration and Monitoring: 1. Administration: Very moist lesions are best treated with nystatin topical dusting powder. For adults and pediatric patients (including neonates), apply liberally to affected areas twice daily or as indicated until healing is complete. 2. Monitoring: Limited information is available regarding monitoring requirements for nystatin. Pharmacology: 1. Mechanism of Action: Nystatin is a polyene antifungal antibiotic that binds to sterols in the cell membrane of susceptible fungi, altering membrane permeability and causing leakage of intracellular components. Resistance to nystatin generally does not develop during therapy, although some Candida species may become resistant and cross-resistant to amphotericin. 2. Pharmacokinetics: Nystatin cream is not absorbed through intact skin or mucous membranes. 3. Microbiology: Nystatin is fungistatic and fungicidal against a variety of yeasts and yeast-like fungi, including Candida albicans. It has no activity against bacteria, protozoa, or viruses. Nonclinical Toxicology: Long-term animal studies to evaluate carcinogenic potential, mutagenicity, or effects on fertility have not been conducted. Storage: Store at 20-25°C (68-77°F). Brand Names: Bio-Statin, Mycostatin, Nystop, Pedi-Dri.
